analysis.one_liner: Halts every not-yet-in-effect Affordable Care Act provision and creates a commission to study its impact.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees in October 2011 and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop, indefinitely, every part of the 2010 health reform law that had not yet taken effect as of the bill's passage — which by late 2011 meant the major 2014 changes: subsidized coverage for the uninsured, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, the insurance mandate, and new taxes on high earners. Federal agencies would be barred from writing or enforcing any rules to carry out those parts. A new ten-member commission would then project what the frozen provisions would have done to Medicare care, insurance coverage, the deficit, and jobs, and report back within 270 days.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, the largest winners would be high-income households, who would avoid the health reform law's pending 3.8% tax on investment income, and health insurers, who would be freed from the not-yet-in-effect market rules (such as guaranteed coverage regardless of pre-existing conditions) even though they would also lose the mandate-driven influx of subsidized customers. Anyone satisfied with the status quo would also be spared the changes scheduled for 2014.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that every provision of the health reform law not yet in effect on enactment 'shall not take effect,' and bars the federal government from promulgating or enforcing regulations under those provisions or preparing to implement them.

It creates an Affordable Care Evaluation Commission of ten politically balanced, nongovernmental appointees with subpoena power, which must report within 270 days on the projected effects of the frozen provisions on Medicare recipients' care, coverage of people already insured, state exchange participation and the deficit, and job creation and the tax base, and recommend corrective measures.
The report must be made available to the public, and the commission terminates 30 days after submitting it.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on people waiting for the law's 2014 coverage expansion: uninsured low- and moderate-income adults who would have gained subsidized coverage or Medicaid, and people with pre-existing conditions who would have gained a guarantee of coverage. Hospitals would continue absorbing uncompensated care from the uninsured. The freeze would also forego the law's revenue provisions, adding to deficits, and taxpayers would fund the new commission.

drawbacks.text: The freeze is not a pause for study — it cancels the law's core benefits on hold indefinitely. The bill text contains no replacement mechanism for covering the uninsured, so the millions expecting 2014 coverage would simply be left out.

The same frozen provisions include the individual mandate and taxes that finance guaranteed coverage for people with pre-existing conditions; blocking them while keeping the law on the books would leave the statute internally unworkable and create legal uncertainty for states and insurers already preparing for 2014.

The commission's assignment is to 'project' future impacts of provisions not yet in effect — speculative work that overlaps with analyses federal agencies and the CBO already produce, at the cost of a new 10-member commission, staff, and subpoena enforcement machinery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — evaluate the law's effects before more of it takes effect — could have been met with a study alone. The mandatory freeze goes much further: it would strip coverage expansion from millions of uninsured Americans, relieve the highest earners of a pending tax, and release insurers from pending consumer protections, all without offering any substitute. The commission's findings could not undo a freeze that had already taken effect, so the study rationale and the freeze's real effects pull in opposite directions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees, whose subcommittees took no action, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Johnson (R-TX) introduced the bill on October 5, 2011, as a Republican effort to halt implementation of the Affordable Care Act.

It was referred the same day to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Appropriations, and Rules — and then parceled out to subcommittees on Health, Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Courts and Administrative Law, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
Only three Republican members cosponsored it; no Democratic support appears in the record.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call at any point; the bill died with the Congress.
Because the freeze never became law, the Affordable Care Act's remaining provisions — including the 2014 coverage expansion — took effect on their original schedule.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Affordable Care Act's pending provisions took effect as scheduled, and the uninsured Americans and high earners whose fates the bill would have shifted were unaffected by it. The bill's aims — freezing the law and forcing a fresh evaluation of it — went unrealized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Uninsured Americans awaiting the law's coverage

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill was part of the Republican effort to stop the Affordable Care Act; no Democrat supported it.

industries.note: A freeze would free insurers from the law's not-yet-in-effect rules, such as guaranteed issue and rating protections, but would also cancel the individual mandate and subsidies that would have delivered them millions of new, publicly subsidized customers. Their interest in this bill genuinely cuts both ways.

The frozen provisions include the 3.8% Medicare contribution tax on investment income for high earners, so the bill's largest direct financial beneficiary is the top slice of households — a gain that comes at the cost of foregone revenue and foregone coverage for the uninsured.

Hospitals counted on the 2014 coverage expansion to reduce uncompensated care; freezing the expansion would leave them treating more uninsured patients at their own expense, alongside the people who would have been covered.
